1.9 Error in Measurement

There is a saying among craftsmen, 'Measure thrice, cut once.' This means that you can reduce the risk of making a mistake in the work by checking the measurement a second or third time before you proceed. In fact it is wise to make any measurement at least three times. Making only one measurement could go completely unnoticed.

Error: All the physical quantities are measurable so accurate measurement is an important part of physics. But the measured value of a physical quantity is usually different from its real value. In other words, we can never make measurements with all certainty and claim that measurements are hundred percent accurate because measurements with all certainty involve a certain error (or uncertainty). We can never take into account the neither instrument may be supposed to be perfect nor any experimenter may be perfect. Since you would not get the same value of x that you try to measure it, your result is obviously uncertain.
The numerical result of a complete measurement is then expressed in the form as
Numerical result = Measured value ± Error
Error = Measured value − Real value
The difference between the measured and the real values of a physical quantity is called error. It is also called uncertainty.
Here x̄ is the mean value of different values measured in the experiment.

For example, if the measured area of your book is 200 ± 0.2 cm². The ± 0.2 cm² ('plus or minus 0.2 cm²') denotes the error in the measurement. The real area of your book most likely lies between 200.2 cm² and 199.8 cm² i.e. the measurement is written as 200 ± 0.2 cm². The correct value of a quantity is not sure so we take the mean value as the correct or true value.
Numerical result = x̄ ± error
Here x̄ is the mean value of different values measured in the experiment.
How to Express an Error?
An error can be expressed by three ways:
(i) Absolute error
(ii) Relative error
(iii) Percentage error
Absolute error: The difference between real value and individual measured value of a physical quantity is called absolute error.
Absolute error = Real value − Measured Value
The correct value of a quantity is not sure so we take the mean value as the correct or real value.
Kinds of Error
Generally, errors in the measurement can be broadly classified into two categories:
(a) Random Errors
(b) Systematic Errors
(a) Random Error
The errors which are due to unknown causes are called random errors. They are also called accidental errors because they are not due to any definite cause.

Causes of Random Error: Random errors arise from the fluctuations that are most easily observed by making multiple trials of a given measurement. For example, if you were to measure the period of a pendulum with a stop watch, you would find that your measurements were not always the same. The main source of these fluctuations would probably be the difficulty of judging exactly when the pendulum came to a given point in its motion, and in starting and stopping the watch at that time. Since you would not get the same value of the period each time that you try to measure it, your result is obviously uncertain.

Minimization of Random Error: Systematic errors are generally 'simple' to analyze but random errors require a more careful judge. Experiments with very small random errors are said to have a high degree of precision. Random errors can be minimized by making a number of readings and then taking their mean.
(b) Systematic Error

The errors which are due to known causes are called systematic errors. The measurement is made under constant condition and hence the error repeats constantly or systematically. So, the error in this category belong to the same sign and always of the same magnitude of the instrument.
Causes of Systematic Error
Bias of the experimenter: Errors in the calibration of the measuring instruments. For example, one might make an incorrect reading because of parallax error.
Incorrect measuring technique: For example, the experimenter might consistently read an instrument incorrectly.

Systematic errors are errors that are constant and always of the same sign and thus may be reduced by averaging over a lot of data. Examples of systematic errors would be time constantly or systematically. So, the error belong to the same category of errors.

All instrumental errors belong to this category. All instrumental errors belong to the constancy of unit. Systematic errors are due to imperfections in the instrument and the imperfections of the instrument condition and hence the error repeats constantly or systematically. So, the error in this category belong to the same category.

Systematic errors are errors that are constant and always of the same sign, such as calibrated instruments. distance measurements by an inaccurately marked meter stick, faulty graduations of a Vernier Calipers and micrometer screw, the end error in a meter bridge, measuring scale etc.
Minimization of Systematic Error

Errors in the calibration of the measuring instruments. For example, one might make an incorrect scale reading because of an instrument incorrectly.
